title: Signature Support Legion
body:
The Signature Support Legion is Manon's original design for a team of support assistants that answers common questions, gathers the details a human needs, and hands hard conversations to a person without delay. A greeter classifies each request, a specialist answers from an approved knowledge base, and a watcher looks for escalation signals: anger, a repeated failure, a refund, or a vulnerable customer. The legion's rule is simple and absolute: a bot never guesses at policy, price, or a promise, and any conversation it cannot answer confidently goes to a human with its notes attached, so the customer never repeats themselves.

Method. The working method for this record is skill routing with a strict handoff rule. First, the greeter classifies the request into billing, technical, or general, and records the customer's channel. Second, the request goes to the specialist bot whose skill matches, or to the human queue when no skill matches. Third, the specialist answers only from the approved knowledge base. Fourth, the watcher checks every turn for escalation signals and hands the conversation to a human the moment one appears. Fifth, the full conversation, including the bot's reasoning and the handoff notes, is logged for audit. The demo routes five fixture requests and escalates the refund request to a human.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature support legion. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: technical | wifi drops daily -> wrench-bot; billing | double charge -> ledger-bot; general | opening hours -> greeter-bot; billing | refund my order -> HUMAN (escalation signal); technical | forgot password -> wrench-bot Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design when a service operation wants faster first answers without removing humans from hard cases, such as order status, password resets, store hours, and return policies. Do not use it for complaints, refunds, medical or legal questions, or any case where a wrong automated answer could cause real harm, and do not let the legion answer from unapproved text. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. The legion operates only on channels its operator owns or is authorized to use, identifies itself as automated where required, never messages people who have not contacted the business or opted in, and respects platform rate limits and human-escalation expectations. The demo below simulates routing locally with fixture tickets; it contacts no real customer.

title: Signature Herald Fleet
body:
The Signature Herald Fleet is Manon's original design for sending alerts people asked for: order updates, appointment reminders, outage notices, and delivery windows. The fleet is built on permission as its first principle: every recipient opted in to a specific kind of message on a specific channel, and the fleet checks that permission before every send, checks quiet hours, and enforces a frequency cap, so no person is ever woken or spammed by a message they wanted. A herald that respects its audience keeps its permission; one that does not loses it, and the design treats that loss as a failure of the fleet, not of the audience.

Method. The working method for this record is opt-in delivery with caps. First, the subscriber list is checked for opt-in to this message type on this channel. Second, quiet hours are checked and messages inside them are held. Third, a per-recipient daily cap is applied. Fourth, the message is composed from an approved template with no advertising added to a transactional alert. Fifth, the send and its result are logged, and any unsubscribe removes the recipient from all future sends immediately. The demo applies these checks to four fixture subscribers and prints send or suppress for each.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature herald fleet. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: eli -> SEND (opted in, under cap); fay -> SUPPRESSED (daily cap reached); gus -> SUPPRESSED (not opted in); hal -> SEND (opted in, under cap) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design when people genuinely want timely updates they asked for, such as delivery windows, appointment reminders, and service outages. Do not use it for marketing to people who did not ask, for messages that ignore quiet hours or caps, or for any list bought, scraped, or collected without clear permission, because that is spam, not notification. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. The herald fleet sends only to opted-in recipients on channels that permit the message type, honors opt-outs instantly, respects per-platform rate limits and template rules, and never reuses a transactional permission for marketing. The demo below simulates these checks locally against a fixture list; it sends nothing to any real person.

title: Signature Watchtower Fleet
body:
The Signature Watchtower Fleet is Manon's original design for watching things that change: whether a website is up, whether a public page changed, whether a status page reports an incident. Each watchtower polls one target on a schedule, compares the new reading with the last, and raises an alert only when something actually changed or failed. The fleet is deliberately patient: it keeps its intervals, backs off when a target struggles, and never hammers a server for a faster answer, because a watchtower that overloads its target becomes the outage it was built to detect.

Method. The working method for this record is scheduled polling with per-host limits. First, each target gets a poll interval and a per-host request budget. Second, the watcher fetches the target's public status and records the result with a timestamp. Third, the new result is compared with the previous one, and only a genuine change or failure produces an alert. Fourth, on repeated failures the watcher lengthens its interval instead of retrying aggressively. Fifth, alerts go to the fleet's own alert channel with the evidence attached, so a human can verify before acting. The demo checks four fixture targets and alerts only on the one that changed.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature watchtower fleet. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: blog -> ok (no change); shop -> ALERT (changed up -> down); status -> ok (no change); docs -> ok (no change) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design when a team needs to know promptly that something it relies on changed or failed, such as its own website, a supplier's status page, or a public data feed it consumes. Do not use it to poll a target that forbids automated access, to ignore rate limits or access controls, or to collect data the target does not publish, because that is not monitoring. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. The watchtower fleet polls only public endpoints and targets it is permitted to check, respects robots rules and published rate limits, identifies itself honestly, and stops immediately when a target asks it to. It never circumvents a login wall, a block, or a paywall. The demo below simulates polls against fixture targets; it contacts no real server.

title: Signature Access Legion
body:
The Signature Access Legion is Manon's original design for making content usable for people who cannot see, hear, or easily read it in its original form. One helper drafts alt-text for images, another drafts captions or transcripts for audio and video, and a third simplifies dense text into plain language. The legion's core rule is that drafts are never published unchecked: every draft goes to a human reviewer with the original attached, because a wrong description can mislead a person who cannot verify it against the original, and the legion exists to increase access, not to publish confident errors.

Method. The working method for this record is draft-then-review assistance. First, the legion takes in content that lacks an accessible alternative. Second, the matching helper produces a draft: a description of the image's content and purpose, a transcript of the audio, or a simplified version of the text. Third, the draft enters a human review queue with the original attached, and nothing publishes until a human approves or corrects it. Fourth, approved alternatives are published alongside the original in the format assistive technology expects. Fifth, coverage is reported, so the team can see which content still lacks an alternative. The demo queues three fixture items and reports coverage before review.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature access legion. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: diagram-1 (chart) -> draft ready -> HUMAN REVIEW QUEUE; lecture-1 (talk) -> draft ready -> HUMAN REVIEW QUEUE; manual-1 (dense text) -> draft ready -> HUMAN REVIEW QUEUE; coverage: 3 items drafted, 0 published before review Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design when a publisher, school, or workplace wants its content to reach people who use screen readers, captions, or plain language, and when human review capacity exists to check drafts. Do not use it to publish unchecked descriptions of important content, such as safety instructions, medical information, or legal notices, where a wrong draft could cause harm. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. The access legion works on content its operator owns or is authorized to adapt, respects licensing and privacy rules, never republishes other people's content without permission, processes user content only with consent, and labels drafts as drafts until a human approves them. The demo below simulates a draft-and-review queue locally with fixture items.

title: Signature Moderation Circle
body:
The Signature Moderation Circle is Manon's original design for helping human moderators keep a community usable by sorting the flood. Helpers scan new posts for signals the community's own published rules care about, such as spam patterns, slurs from a published blocklist, or links to known scam domains, and sort posts into queues: clearly fine, needs a human look, or urgent. The circle never bans, deletes, or judges on its own; it only organizes the work so humans decide faster and with better evidence, because moderation without a human decision and an appeal is not moderation at all.

Method. The working method for this record is flag-and-queue triage. First, each new post is checked against the community's published rules and signal lists, and every signal is recorded with the rule it matches. Second, posts with no signals pass untouched. Third, posts with signals go to a human review queue ordered by severity, with the matched signals shown as evidence. Fourth, the human moderator decides: allow, warn, remove, or ban, and the decision and reason are logged. Fifth, appealed decisions return to a different human, never to the helper that flagged the post. The demo triages four fixture posts and sends two to human review.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature moderation circle. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 'welcome to the forum' -> PASS (no signals); 'free money click here' -> HUMAN REVIEW QUEUE (signals: spam-pattern); 'thanks for the help' -> PASS (no signals); 'claim your prize at scam-site.example' -> HUMAN REVIEW QUEUE (signals: scam-domain) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design when a community has more posts than its moderators can read in order and wants its humans to spend time on judgment rather than sorting. Do not use it to auto-ban, auto-delete, or shadow-ban users, to enforce secret rules, or to target people for their opinions. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. The moderation circle operates only in communities its operator runs or is authorized to moderate, under rules published to that community, and within the host platform's moderation and automation policies. It must not scrape or monitor communities it does not run, must not profile users across communities, and must keep its signal lists and decisions auditable. The demo below simulates triage locally on fixture posts; it bans nobody.

title: Signature Polite Crawler Fleet
body:
The Signature Polite Crawler Fleet is Manon's original design for gathering public web material for research by fetching pages the way a polite guest would: it reads each site's robots rules, waits between requests, identifies itself honestly, and stops when asked. The fleet spreads work across several crawler bots, each responsible for a set of sites, so no single site is hit by the whole fleet at once. Researchers use such fleets to build corpora, track public information over time, and preserve public pages, and the fleet's politeness is what keeps that work welcome.

Method. The working method for this record is robots-respecting crawling with per-site budgets. First, before any fetch, the crawler reads the site's robots file and records which paths are allowed and what crawl delay is requested. Second, each site gets a request budget and a delay between requests, and the fleet never exceeds either. Third, every request carries an honest user-agent string naming the crawler and a contact, so a site owner can reach a human. Fourth, any disallowed path, any block, or any request to stop is honored immediately and permanently for that site. Fifth, fetched pages are stored with their source and fetch time, so research built on them can be checked. The demo decides crawl or skip for three fixture sites.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature polite crawler fleet. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: public-library.example -> CRAWL ALLOWED, delay 3s between requests; open-journal.example -> CRAWL ALLOWED, delay 10s between requests; members-only.example -> SKIP (robots rules disallow) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design when research genuinely needs public web material at scale and the sites permit automated access, such as archiving public pages, studying public discourse, or building a corpus of public documents. Do not use it on sites that forbid crawling, behind logins or paywalls, against rate limits or blocks, or to collect personal data, because that is not research crawling. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. The polite crawler fleet fetches only public pages on sites whose robots rules allow it, obeys crawl delays and request budgets, never circumvents access controls, and honors opt-outs and takedown requests. It does not collect personal data and does not republish fetched material beyond what the source's terms and the law allow. The demo below simulates robots-rule decisions locally on fixture sites; it fetches no real page.

title: Signature Task Marshal
body:
The Signature Task Marshal is Manon's original design for the dispatcher at the center of a bot army: work arrives as tasks in a queue, and the marshal hands each task to a bot that is idle, capable, and healthy, then watches for the result. When a bot fails a task, the marshal retries it a limited number of times, and when retries are exhausted the task goes to a dead-letter queue where a human can inspect it, instead of the fleet silently dropping the work or retrying forever. The marshal is what separates a fleet from a crowd: the same bots with a marshal finish more work, lose less of it, and can say exactly where every task went.

Method. The working method for this record is queue-based assignment with bounded retries. First, tasks enter a queue carrying their type and a retry count starting at zero. Second, the marshal assigns each task to an idle bot whose declared skills include the task type, preferring the least-loaded such bot. Third, the marshal waits for a success or failure report within a timeout; a timeout counts as a failure. Fourth, a failed task returns to the queue with its retry count increased, up to a fixed maximum, and a task that exceeds the maximum moves to the dead-letter queue with its failure history attached. Fifth, the marshal publishes counts of assigned, completed, retried, and dead-lettered tasks so the fleet's health is visible. The demo assigns six fixture tasks and dead-letters one.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature task marshal. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: a1 -> marshal-bot-1 COMPLETED; a2 -> marshal-bot-2 COMPLETED; a3 -> marshal-bot-1 FAILED, retry 1 -> marshal-bot-1 FAILED, retry 2 -> DEAD-LETTER QUEUE; a4 -> marshal-bot-2 COMPLETED; a5 -> marshal-bot-1 COMPLETED; a6 -> marshal-bot-2 COMPLETED; summary: assigned 6, completed 5, dead-lettered 1 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design whenever several bots share work that must not be lost, such as processing queues, answering channels, or running scheduled jobs. Do not use it for work that must happen exactly once unless the tasks themselves are idempotent, because retries can otherwise repeat side effects, and do not let a marshal hide failures by retrying without limit. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. The marshal operates only on work its operator owns or is authorized to process, and assigns tasks only to bots the operator controls. It logs every assignment and outcome, never assigns work that accesses systems or data without authorization, and respects the rate limits of any downstream service its bots call. The demo below simulates assignment locally with fixture tasks and one failing bot; it processes no real work.

title: Signature Throttle Guard
body:
The Signature Throttle Guard is Manon's original design for keeping a bot fleet a good citizen of every service it calls: each bot, or the fleet as a whole, holds a budget of requests per window, and when the budget runs out the fleet waits instead of pushing through. When a service answers with a slow-down signal, the guard backs off exponentially, waiting longer after each refusal, instead of retrying immediately and turning a busy service into a failed one. Platforms publish their limits precisely because fleets that ignore them get blocked, and a fleet that respects them keeps working for years while an aggressive one is shut off in a day.

Method. The working method for this record is a token bucket with exponential backoff, simulated locally. First, the fleet holds a bucket of tokens for each downstream service, refilled at the service's published rate, and every request spends one token. Second, a request with no token available is queued, not sent, until the bucket refills. Third, when a service refuses a request, the guard records the refusal and multiplies its wait time before the next attempt, up to a cap. Fourth, after a run of successes the wait time decays back toward normal. Fifth, the guard logs allowed, queued, and refused requests per service so operators can see which budget is tight and adjust schedules instead of raising limits unilaterally. The demo runs a small bucket for eight ticks.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature throttle guard. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: tick 0 -> REQUEST ALLOWED, tokens left: 2; tick 1 -> REQUEST ALLOWED, tokens left: 2; tick 2 -> REQUEST ALLOWED, tokens left: 2; tick 3 -> REQUEST ALLOWED, tokens left: 2; tick 4 -> REQUEST ALLOWED, tokens left: 2; tick 5 -> REQUEST ALLOWED, tokens left: 2; tick 6 -> REQUEST ALLOWED, tokens left: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design for every fleet that calls an outside service, a platform API, or a shared resource, because limits are a fact of online operation, not an optional courtesy. Do not use it to justify exceeding a limit by spreading requests across accounts, bots, or addresses, because that is evasion, and a fleet caught evading loses its access entirely. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. Rate limiting is itself an authorization rule: a fleet may use only the budget the service grants it, must honor slow-down and retry-after signals, and must never split traffic across identities to multiply its allowance. The pattern assumes the fleet's API access is authorized in the first place; an unauthorized caller with a polite rate limit is still unauthorized. The demo below simulates a token bucket locally; it calls no real service.

title: Signature Lifeline Fleet
body:
The Signature Lifeline Fleet is Manon's original design for how a bot army survives losing a member: every bot sends regular heartbeats, the coordinator watches for silence, and when a bot misses enough heartbeats it is declared unhealthy, its unfinished tasks are taken back, and they are reassigned to healthy bots. Without a lifeline, a dead bot is a black hole: work assigned to it waits forever and nobody notices. With one, the fleet degrades gracefully, losing capacity but never losing track of the work, and the failed bot can rejoin later once it is healthy again, after proving itself with a fresh heartbeat streak.

Method. The working method for this record is heartbeat monitoring with redistribution. First, each bot sends a heartbeat every interval, and the coordinator records the time of the last heartbeat per bot. Second, a bot that misses two consecutive heartbeats is marked unhealthy and stops receiving new tasks. Third, the unhealthy bot's unfinished tasks return to the queue with their retry counts preserved, so they are reassigned rather than duplicated blindly. Fourth, healthy bots absorb the returned work within their capacity limits, and the coordinator reports the fleet's reduced capacity honestly. Fifth, a recovered bot must send a streak of healthy heartbeats before it receives work again, so a flapping bot cannot thrash the queue. The demo checks three fixture bots and redistributes one bot's work.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature lifeline fleet. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: life-bot-1 -> HEALTHY; life-bot-2 -> UNHEALTHY (missed 3 heartbeats), tasks redistributed; life-bot-3 -> HEALTHY Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design for any fleet where a bot can crash, lose its network, or be restarted, which is to say every real fleet. Do not use it as an excuse to run a fleet with no capacity headroom, because failover redistributes work but does not create capacity, and do not let a repeatedly failing bot rejoin without diagnosis. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. Failover changes only which authorized bot does authorized work; it never grants a bot new permissions, new data access, or a new identity. A replacement bot inherits exactly the failed bot's authorized scope, and the redistribution is logged like every other assignment. The demo below simulates heartbeats locally with fixture bots; it controls no real fleet.

title: Signature Seal Verifier Fleet
body:
The Signature Seal Verifier Fleet is Manon's original design for taking in event notifications from other services safely: a payment provider reporting a completed payment, a repository reporting a new release, a store reporting a shipment. The danger of event webhooks is forgery, because anyone who learns the endpoint can send fake events, so every legitimate sender seals its payloads with a shared secret, and the verifier checks the seal before trusting a single byte. The fleet also guards against replays, because a genuine event delivered twice must not charge a customer twice or publish a release twice.

Method. The working method for this record is HMAC verification with idempotency. First, the verifier reads the event's identifier, timestamp, and signature header before touching the payload. Second, it recomputes the HMAC seal over the raw payload with the shared secret and compares it in constant time with the presented seal; any mismatch means the event is rejected and logged, never processed. Third, the event identifier is checked against the store of already-processed identifiers, and a replay is acknowledged but not reprocessed. Fourth, a fresh, verified event is processed exactly once and its identifier is recorded. Fifth, the verifier answers promptly with a success code so the sender does not retry a finished event. The demo verifies three fixture events: one good, one forged, one replay.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature seal verifier fleet. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: s-1 -> VERIFIED, PROCESSED: order shipped; s-2 -> REJECTED (bad seal); s-1 -> ACKNOWLEDGED, NOT REPROCESSED (replay) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design whenever a fleet must react to events from another service, such as payments, shipments, code releases, or form submissions. Do not use it without seal verification, without idempotency, or with a shared secret stored where it can leak, because an unverified event endpoint is an open door to anyone who finds it. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. The seal verifier fleet accepts events only from senders it has a configured relationship with, over the sender's documented signing scheme, and it keeps shared secrets in a proper secret store, never in code or logs. It must reject unsigned, mis-signed, and stale events, and it must never act on an event to access a system the fleet is not authorized for. The demo below verifies seals locally on fixture payloads with a test secret; it receives no real webhooks.

title: Signature Channel Legion
body:
The Signature Channel Legion is Manon's original design for letting one assistant serve people wherever they already are: on a website chat, inside a messaging app, by email, and by voice, without making each channel a separate project. A single conversation core holds the assistant's knowledge and rules, while a thin adapter per channel translates between the core and the channel's format, buttons, and limits. The hard part is not the adapters but the rules: each channel has its own opt-in requirements, message formats, rate limits, and expectations, and the legion honors the strictest applicable rule for every message rather than the most convenient one.

Method. The working method for this record is core-plus-adapters routing with per-channel rule checks. First, an incoming message arrives through its channel adapter, which normalizes it into the core's format and records the channel, the sender's opt-in state, and the channel's constraints. Second, the core produces a reply from the approved knowledge base, exactly as it would on any channel. Third, before sending, the channel adapter checks the reply against that channel's rules: opt-in status, message-type permission, template requirements, length limits, and rate budget. Fourth, a reply that fails any check is held, rewritten to a compliant form, or routed to a human, and the decision is logged. Fifth, the conversation state is shared across channels, so a person who starts on chat and continues by email is not asked the same questions twice. The demo routes fixture messages across three channels.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature channel legion. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: site-chat -> SEND (opted in, under cap); messenger -> HELD (no opt-in on this channel); email -> HELD (channel rate cap reached) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design when an audience genuinely lives on several channels and expects consistent answers on each. Do not use it to carry a permission from one channel into another, to spam a channel where the person never opted in, or to hide the fact that the assistant is automated where a channel requires disclosure. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. The channel legion needs separate authorization per channel: a business-messaging approval on each messaging platform, a confirmed opt-in list for email, and the website chat it owns. Permissions never transfer between channels, and each channel's rate limits, template rules, and disclosure rules apply to its own messages. The demo below simulates routing locally with fixture channels and permissions; it sends nothing anywhere.

title: Signature Publisher Fleet
body:
The Signature Publisher Fleet is Manon's original design for preparing posts, articles, and announcements in advance and releasing them on a timetable, with a human approval gate standing between every draft and the public. One helper drafts from approved sources and templates, another checks the draft against style, factual, and policy rules, and a third holds the draft until its scheduled time, releasing it only if a human has approved it. The approval gate is the whole point: a fleet that publishes without a human looking has no one to blame when it publishes an error, and a fleet with a gate gets both the speed of automation and the judgment of an editor.

Method. The working method for this record is draft, check, approve, release. First, drafts are created from approved sources and templates, each carrying its source references and its scheduled time. Second, an automated checker screens each draft for style violations, missing sources, and flagged claims, and returns failures for revision. Third, a draft that passes the screen enters the human approval queue, where an editor approves, edits, or rejects it. Fourth, at the scheduled time, the release helper publishes only drafts marked approved, and only to the channels listed on the approval. Fifth, every published item keeps its draft, its checks, and its approver attached, so any published error can be traced to its exact origin and corrected publicly. The demo runs three fixture drafts through the pipeline.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature publisher fleet. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: release-1 -> RELEASED (checked and approved); release-2 -> HELD (failed automated check); release-3 -> HELD (awaiting human approval) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design when an organization publishes regularly and wants a reliable timetable without surrendering editorial control, such as announcements, newsletters, and documentation releases. Do not use it to publish unreviewed claims, to flood a channel with automated posts, or to impersonate a person, because scheduled publishing without approval is spam with a calendar. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. The publisher fleet publishes only to accounts and channels its operator owns or is authorized to manage, under each platform's automation and publishing policies, and it must identify automated posts as required. It must not publish to accounts it does not control, must not evade a platform's posting limits, and must keep the human approval gate for anything that makes claims about people, products, or events. The demo below simulates the pipeline locally with fixture drafts; it publishes nothing.

title: Signature Translation Fleet
body:
The Signature Translation Fleet is Manon's original design for carrying conversations across languages: a customer writes in one language, the fleet translates for the support team, the team replies in its own language, and the fleet translates back. The fleet is built for the reality that machine translation is good at ordinary sentences and unreliable at exactly the places where reliability matters most: names, numbers, medical or legal terms, and anything emotional. So the fleet translates freely for routine content and routes sensitive content to a human reviewer before it reaches the other side, trading a little speed for the accuracy that trust requires.

Method. The working method for this record is translate with sensitivity routing. First, each incoming message is classified as routine or sensitive, using keyword lists for medical, legal, financial, and safety topics plus any user-set flag. Second, routine messages are translated by the fleet's translation service and delivered with a note that they are machine-translated. Third, sensitive messages go to a human reviewer fluent in both languages, who corrects the translation before delivery. Fourth, names, numbers, dates, and quoted terms are preserved verbatim through translation and highlighted for the reviewer. Fifth, every translation keeps its source text attached, so either side can check what was actually said. The demo routes three fixture phrases.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature translation fleet. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 'good morning, I need help' -> TRANSLATED: bonjour, jai besoin daide; 'my blood pressure medicine dose' -> HUMAN REVIEW QUEUE (sensitive content); 'thanks, that solved it' -> TRANSLATED: merci, cela a resolu le probleme Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design when people who do not share a language need to work together and routine translation would genuinely help, such as customer support, community forums, and classrooms. Do not use it for medical instructions, legal notices, safety warnings, or contracts without human review, and do not present a machine translation as a certified translation, because it is not one. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. The translation fleet processes messages only with the consent of the conversation's participants, under the privacy rules of the channel it serves, and it must not store or reuse conversation content beyond what its operators disclose. It must never translate private messages it was not invited into, and its machine-translated output must be labeled as such. The demo below simulates the pipeline locally with fixture phrases; it translates nothing for any real person.

title: Signature API Harvest Fleet
body:
The Signature API Harvest Fleet is Manon's original design for gathering data a team is entitled to use from several services at once and turning it into one report: sales from the store's API, shipping status from the carrier's API, and inventory from the warehouse's API, combined into a single morning summary. Each source is accessed through its own authorized API key with its own quota, and the fleet's job is to stay inside every quota, normalize the different formats into one shape, and say plainly which sources answered and which did not, so a report built on partial data never pretends to be complete.

Method. The working method for this record is quota-aware aggregation with provenance. First, the fleet lists the sources for the report and checks each source's authorization, quota remaining, and rate limit before calling anything. Second, it calls the authorized APIs in priority order, stopping at any source's quota rather than borrowing quota from another identity. Third, each response is normalized into the report's common shape, with the source and fetch time attached to every row. Fourth, sources that failed or were skipped for quota are listed as missing, and the report states its own completeness. Fifth, the finished report is delivered to its authorized audience and the quota usage is logged per source. The demo aggregates three fixture sources with quotas.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature api harvest fleet. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: shop-api -> FETCHED (quota 2/5 remaining); ship-api -> SKIPPED (quota exhausted, reported as missing); stock-api -> FETCHED (quota 4/5 remaining); report completeness: 2 of 3 sources present Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design when a team needs one view across several services it legitimately uses, such as sales, shipping, and inventory, or public data from open APIs. Do not use it to aggregate data the team is not authorized for, to scrape what an API deliberately does not offer, to exceed a quota by rotating keys or accounts, or to combine data in ways that defeat a source's privacy rules. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. The harvest fleet uses only APIs it is authorized for, with its own credentials, inside each API's quota and terms, and it honors each source's redistribution and privacy rules for the combined output. It must never present another service's data as its own, must attribute sources, and must stop at a source's limit rather than evading it. The demo below aggregates simulated API fixtures locally with a quota; it calls no real API.

title: Signature Welcome Fleet
body:
The Signature Welcome Fleet is Manon's original design for welcoming new users and walking them to their first success: it asks what they want to do, shows the shortest path to it, explains the first screen, and stays nearby for the next question. The fleet is a set of guide helpers organized as a decision tree: one greeter asks the goal, others cover each goal's path, and every path ends either in the user doing the thing or in a human helper. Good welcoming is measured by whether new users actually succeed, not by how many messages the fleet sent, so the fleet tracks completion and hands off the moment a user stalls.

Method. The working method for this record is decision-tree guidance with stall detection. First, the greeter asks the new user's goal in plain language and offers the three most common goals as choices. Second, the matching guide walks the user step by step, one action per message, checking after each step whether the user completed it. Third, when the user completes the path, the fleet confirms the success and offers the natural next step. Fourth, when the user stalls twice, answers off-path, or asks for a person, the fleet hands the conversation to a human with the path taken so far attached. Fifth, completion and handoff rates are reported per path, and paths with low completion are rewritten. The demo guides three fixture answers.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature welcome fleet. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: create account -> guide: profile -> verify -> done; find a document -> guide: search -> open -> done; speak to a human -> HUMAN HANDOFF (user asked for a person) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design when new users must learn a product, service, or process and a guided first run would genuinely help, such as setting up an account, placing a first order, or using a new tool. Do not use it to trap users in a bot loop, to hide the way to a human, or to push users toward purchases they did not ask about, because welcoming that frustrates is churn with extra steps. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. The welcome fleet operates only on its operator's own product or service, with the user's consent to be guided, and it must always offer a visible path to a human. It must not collect data beyond what onboarding needs, must not guide users into purchases or permissions under false pretenses, and must respect the channel's automation and disclosure rules. The demo below simulates guidance locally with fixture answers; it guides no real user.

title: Signature Ledger Fleet
body:
The Signature Ledger Fleet is Manon's original design for writing down everything a bot army does so that any action can be explained later: every task assigned, every message sent, every API call made, every decision to escalate, and every failure, each with its time, its bot, its reason, and its result. A ledger turns a fleet from an inscrutable swarm into an accountable system: when a customer asks why they received a message, when a platform asks why a rate limit was hit, or when an operator asks why a task failed, the ledger answers with evidence instead of guesses. A fleet without a ledger cannot prove it behaved, and in a dispute, that is the same as not having behaved.

Method. The working method for this record is append-only logging with periodic audit reports. First, every bot action emits a structured log entry carrying a timestamp, a bot identifier, an action type, a target reference, an authorization reference, and an outcome. Second, log entries are written to append-only storage that ordinary bots cannot rewrite, so history cannot be edited after the fact. Third, a daily audit job summarizes the logs: actions per bot, sends per channel, failures per type, and escalations, and flags anomalies such as one bot's error rate spiking or a channel's volume doubling overnight. Fourth, flagged anomalies go to a human operator with the evidence attached, never to an automated punishment. Fifth, logs are retained for the period the operator's policy states, then deleted, because a ledger is a record, not a hoard. The demo audits a small fixture log and flags one anomaly.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record is a local simulation that carries out a concrete run for signature ledger fleet. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: ledger-bot-1 escalate ok x1; ledger-bot-1 send ok x1; ledger-bot-2 send failed x2; anomaly flagged: ledger-bot-2 failed 2 sends in a row -> HUMAN OPERATOR REVIEW Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet. No part of the demo goes online, messages anyone, scrapes anything, or attacks anything.

Use and limits. Use this design for every fleet that touches customers, platforms, or money, because accountability is not optional at that scale. Do not use logging as surveillance of people: log the fleet's actions and the minimum necessary references, not the content of private conversations, and do not keep logs longer than policy allows. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

Authorization and platform rules. Authorization and platform rules. Ledger logging is itself governed by privacy rules: it records what the fleet did, not the private content it handled, and access to logs is restricted to authorized operators for stated purposes. Log storage must respect data-retention and deletion duties, and audit reports must not expose one customer's data to another. The demo below generates a small fixture log locally and prints its audit summary; it logs no real activity.
